title: Sanctifying the name
hookLine: sometimes by martyrdom, but usually by living so others respect God

lines: A DONKEY, A TRADER, A JEWEL.
cards: A teacher hauls flax for a living, and his students want to spare him the work, so they buy him a donkey from a trader. Back home, they find a precious stone hanging from its neck.
Now, they say, their teacher can stop working so hard. He asks one question. Does the seller know?
No. Then take it back, he says; he bought a donkey, not a jewel. So the stone goes back, and the trader holds it and says, in effect: blessed is the God of this teacher.

teach.h: A STORY FROM THE JERUSALEM TALMUD.
teach.b: The story is in the Jerusalem Talmud, and the rabbi is Shimon ben Shetach. Kiddush Hashem means sanctifying the name, the name of God. Its opposite is chillul Hashem, profaning the name.
The rabbis tie both to a verse in Leviticus, where God says: "I will be hallowed among the children of Israel."
Notice where the hallowing happens: among people.
Yesterday's Rhineland chroniclers used this phrase for those who died rather than give up their faith, and Jewish tradition honors them with it.
Jewish law also teaches that saving a life comes first, and asks for martyrdom only in rare and terrible cases.
And the rabbis teach an everyday kind too. In the Babylonian Talmud, in tractate Yoma, the sage Abaye puts it this way: let the name of Heaven become beloved because of you.
Someone who studies, deals honestly in the market and speaks gently with people makes others say, how fine are this person's ways, and fortunate is the one who taught them. The reverse holds too.
A person known for learning who cheats or is rude makes people think less of the teaching. So the name of God, in this view, travels with people's behavior.
A returned jewel, a fair price, a kind word to a stranger: each is a small Kiddush Hashem. That is why a martyr's death and a shopkeeper's honest scale can share one phrase.

how: Jewish teachers often remind people that honest business, kindness and courtesy are a Kiddush Hashem, and that dishonest conduct by a religious person is a chillul Hashem, a profaning of the name.

o: a blessing said over wine to start Shabbat
sanctifying God's name, by a life or a death
saying God's name aloud in a holy place

p: sent the jewel back to the trader
let Heaven's name become beloved through you

s: Kiddush Hashem only means dying for one's faith
the rabbis also apply it to honest, kind everyday conduct.
the Leviticus verse says God will be hallowed among the children of Israel
the hallowing happens among people, which is where the idea starts.
the same Talmud passage warns that a learned person's bad behavior lowers respect for the teaching
that is chillul Hashem, the opposite of sanctifying the name.

games.q: you are Shimon ben Shetach's student. you have just bought your teacher a donkey, and a jewel is hanging from its neck. the seller doesn't know. what does your teacher say?
o: it came with the donkey, so keep it.
sell it and give the money to charity.
take it back: he bought a donkey, not a jewel.
games.why: he sent it back, and the trader blessed the God of Shimon ben Shetach.

practice: Run through the rest of your day: the people you'll meet, the messages you'll send, the line at the store.
Choose one moment where you could be a little more honest, more patient or more generous than anyone expects, and see yourself doing it.

wordCard.voice: Kiddush Hashem. Sanctifying the name: sometimes, in the worst times, by dying for it, and far more often by living in a way that makes others respect it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: sanctify the name by living. Mostly it happens in small, honest moments. Day nine hundred thirty-seven, done.
